> This custom audio synthesizer is a low-cost, standalone electronic music instrument built around an RP2040 microcontroller. It will feature eight playable keys, octave controls, a mode-selection button, two rotary encoders, and a built-in speaker. The project combines embedded programming, audio electronics, custom PCB design, and enclosure design. My goal is to build an affordable synthesizer capable of generating electronic sounds through physical controls while documenting the complete design and build process.

## Design

### 2026-10-20 – To start off with my project, I created the github repository, drafted ideas on what I should make, and went online to find for vendors that sell the components that I need to build my audio synthesiz

**2.28h**

To start off with my project, I created the github repository, drafted ideas on what I should make, and went online to find for vendors that sell the components that I need to build my audio synthesizer.

I landed on the idea to create an audio synthesizer because I thought that we had to create something like a synth, until it changed to an instrument week. After doing research online on what a synth is and how it works, I decided that creating my own would seem like a really cool project and I can definitely use it to play some music when I am bored or have nothing else better to do, a replacement for doomscrolling I suppose. I drew a few sketches for my audio synthesizer, I wanted it to be able to play different instruments with the use of just 8 keys ranging from C, D, E, F, G, A, B and C, which are the keys for an octave starting from the middle C. My synthesizer would have a potentiometer to change the volume of playing, 2 rotary encoders to change the tone of the instrument that I am using, 3 buttons, one for changing the instrument, one for going one octave down and another for going one octave up, and one screen to show the volume, tone, which part of the  piano I'm playing and the type of instrument I'm currently using.

Hence, after getting my idea, I immediately went to KiCAD and started designing the schematics and PCB, I found a github repository that contains the footprint and symbol to the SSD1306 0.96 inch OLED screen, making it perfect for me to identify the dimensions of the screen when I design the CAD enclosure. Completing my PCB design.

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/466c9673-92f7-40a7-9de3-5bcb5ec476e7/video.mp4)

### 2026-10-20 – After finishing the PCB design, I realized that I forgot to put the CAD model of my screen in the KiCAD footprint library thing, and I haven't put the potentiometer in yet. I went back to KiCAD, gathe

**0.72h**

After finishing the PCB design, I realized that I forgot to put the CAD model of my screen in the KiCAD footprint library thing, and I haven't put the potentiometer in yet. I went back to KiCAD, gathered information about the potentiometer that I'm using and then connecting the wires for that potentiometer to the RP2040 Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller chip that I'm using for this audio synthesizer. The extra 30 minutes was not recorded as I thought that it would be a very short process (I was wrong)...

### 2026-10-20 – After finishing my audio synthesizer design, I moved on to making the firmware, and that's when I realized that the numbering for my key buttons are incorrect, with the row 3 column 2 matrix in the sc

**1.75h**

After finishing my audio synthesizer design, I moved on to making the firmware, and that's when I realized that the numbering for my key buttons are incorrect, with the row 3 column 2 matrix in the schematic being SW11 instead of SW10, which is quite a big problem as I duplicated those with the diodes along with them, needing to change the values of the diodes, and making changes to how the buttons are arranged on the audio synthesizer as they are changed already in the schematic, it took me a good 30 or 40 minutes working on rearranging the buttons and connecting the tracks again. In my opinion, the tracks are one of the most difficult thing to do when designing a PCB, never really liked that part, but it always turns our fantastic once you're done with it.

But obviously I can't spend a whole hour and 3 quarters just redesigning the entire PCB right? After completing the redesigning I went on to code the firmware that is needed to make  the keyboard work. In the coding part I used some of ChatGPT's help with some part of the code, like debugging and all, to which most of the other parts are written by myself with some help from my teachers.
